A September 2026 study in Critical Care Explorations (Seifi & Seyfi) tested 300 neurocritical care references generated from memory by GPT-5.3, Grok-4, and DeepSeek-V3:  • 55.0% contained citation inaccuracies • 28.3% were completely fabricated — papers that don't exist • GPT-5.3: 69% inaccurate (27% fabricated) • Grok-4: 73% inaccurate (50% fabricated) • DeepSeek-V3: 23% inaccurate (8% fabricated) And even when a DOI points to a real paper, subtle errors slip through — a wrong first author, a shifted hazard ratio, or a paper that was retracted years ago. Using AI to help draft research isn't the problem. Publishing unverified citations is — and asking another LLM to "double-check its sources" isn't the fix. So I built ref-verify — a free, open-source, purely deterministic Python CLI and AI agent skill that verifies scientific citations against live primary databases. No LLM in the verification loop, no guesswork. How it works:  Point it at a single citation + claim (ref-verify check), a bibliography JSON (ref-verify batch), or an entire .docx, .pptx, or .md draft (ref-verify scan).  It deterministically extracts and normalizes every DOI and PMID, then cross-checks them live against Crossref, PubMed, and Europe PMC.  Instead of a vague pass/fail, it outputs exact pinpointing diagnostics (Expected, Actual, Hint, Fix), flags retracted papers and editorial notices, and diffs the numbers in your claim (HRs, 95% CIs, p-values, sample sizes) against the official abstract or open-access full text — so you or your AI agent can fix everything in one pass. Researchers studying treatment effects want to understand how estimates might differ among patients with different medical histories. The authors trained an AI model on past health records from about three hundred fifty thousand participants in the United States All of Us research program. It learns patterns from diagnosis and medication histories and uses them to estimate how treatment effects might vary across individuals. The authors tested the method retrospectively in comparisons involving diabetes and cancer treatments. Their results appear in a preprint that has yet to undergo peer review. Loop is internally called Jitro; interestingly, that was the exact name for Jules v2.   Here is how it works 👀  1. Users start creating a Workspace by connecting it to a selected Github project and adding basic information.   2. Users can create loops manually or select ones that are already predefined (ex., Harden Application Security)  "Custom Loops" can be created via a prompt or by manually filling in the Loop title, icon, and objective.   > "Loops are mid- to long-term objectives for Stitch Loop to continuously work toward. They can range from highly specific to broad, but should always be something code can achieve," says the description.   3. Users can connect additional context in the form of Integrations, Files, Links, or additional repositories.  More than 100 integrations are available there, including services like Jira, Linear, Datadog, Sentry, Notion, Snowflake, Salesforce, Intercom, Discord, Slack, Figma, and many others.   Custom MCPs are supported as well.   4. After creating a workspace, Loop will start digging into your project details and generate its own Skills about the product and product metrics.   These Skills will live in a separate tab and can be edited in the UI in Markdown.   5. When the Workspace is ready, Loop will suggest metrics and goals based on its own research. Users can convert these suggestions into loops right away.   When a Loop is created, it appears as a running process in the main UI.   6. When a Loop is finished, users will see a list of suggestions for every loop, along with a number associated with a target metric and progress status.   Example Loop: - Goal - Scale Telegram community contributions. - KPIs - community members, registered contributors, active members.   A high-level goal would be broken down into sub-KPIs. When users open a dedicated Loop page, all these KPIs will be visible on the dashboard.  Below, Users will see a list of Tasks, Skills, and Activity tabs.   Example Task: - Telegram channel lacks discussion threads and a dedicated bot.  Each task has a detailed description, labels, and the date when it was updated. Below, users will see tabs for Solutions, Activity, and Evidence.   Activity appears as a summary describing what happened, what was done, and the general Timeline.   Evidence contains links to where Loop pulled the context behind this Task. In my example case, it refers to the TestingCatalog website and the Telegram channel from which it pulled all the numbers.   Example Solution:  - Dedicated Telegram Bot API intake bot with editorial triage webhook (implementation task).   This task is an implementation task that has a clear description, Impact, scope, and Risk labeled.   Users can start the task right from this page to begin solution development via Gemini.   When the task is done, users can review its progress and status and monitor its impact on production by pulling updated metrics and KPIs after the release.   What does all this mean? 🤯  Loop follows how "Product work" is done at Google, a model many other companies also use.  Every Workspace in Loop is equivalent to a scope that is normally handled by a complete product engineering team.   It is no longer a place where users play the role of engineering lead and product lead, orchestrating AI agents.  It is a place where the user plays the role of a senior manager managing several engineering teams, which is a big shift on its own.   We are slowly moving towards autonomous AI organizations. One management layer at a time.  I expect it will still take until 2027 for labs to develop the products and models needed to make substantial progress in this area (assuming AI continues to advance in a semi-regulated format as it is now). XI|2026-11-22 10:27|https://x.com/Ownerthoughts/status/2124449615122411606|https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2124447171063787520/vid/avc1/1080x1350/osnCOqrwe41FpO2K.mp4?tag=29|https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2124447171063787520/img/-ByNAL_MZjnsNIu3.jpg|30|103|A Week Without a Single Purchase: How I Tested AI Agents Before Entrusting Them with a Single Dollar  On the first day, I was itching to get started. The agents were configured, the wallet was funded, and potential leads were already popping up in the chat. All it would have taken was the press of a single button to set the whole system into live trading mode.  I didn’t press it. For the first seven days, my team followed one rule: don’t buy anything—just log what the agents *would* have done. It’s a tedious process, and I wouldn’t recommend any of my other ideas—but this one, I highly endorse.  Below, I’ll explain exactly what I was testing, where the system was deceiving itself, and the specific indicators I used to decide whether it could finally be trusted with real money—or if it couldn’t.  Shadow Mode: How It Works  The agents operate as usual: a scout identifies leads, an auditor vets them, and an executor prepares the order. But there’s no final sign-off; instead of being executed, the order is simply logged. The entry includes the token, price, position size, stop-loss, and the rationale for the trade.  After an hour, a day, and three days, I compare these logged decisions against what actually happened in the market. This process doesn’t cost a single dollar. Yet, after a week, I had a record of nine trading decisions—and a sobering realization of just how little I actually knew about my own system.  What I measured  Looking at daily PnL on paper is pointless: in a good week, almost anyone’s PnL will look impressive. I measured something else.  Address consistency. A contract address should appear identical across the scout, the auditor, and the executor. I manually investigated every discrepancy; there were five such instances over the course of a week. Each one represented a potential loss of funds.  Reasons for rejection. I didn’t just look at how many tokens were filtered out, but why. If 90% of rejections stem from the same reason, it suggests that the other checks are either non-functional or entirely useless.  Timing of leads. This is the most problematic metric. A scout might identify a perfect token, but if the price has already surged, entering a position effectively means buying someone else’s exit. I compared the time a lead appeared against the subsequent price movement.  Unexplained silence. If an agent remains silent for two days, it could simply be a quiet market—or it could mean a data source has broken. I verified that every silent agent could provide a log of what it had checked and why it hadn’t found anything.  Frequency of required human intervention. If a system asks for my input on every minor detail, it isn’t saving me any time. Conversely, if it never asks for anything, I suspect it doesn’t actually know where the boundaries lie.  A Trap I Nearly Fell Into  On the third day, I noticed that a token rejected by the auditor had surged in value. My first thought was obvious: the auditor was being too cautious—the filters needed to be relaxed.  Then, I opened the log and read the reason for the rejection: "minting rights have not been revoked." The check turned out to be correct. The token had risen, but it could have collapsed at any moment—and, in fact, it did crash two hours later (I don’t know what happened to it after that).  A single positive outcome proves nothing about the validity of a decision. If you evaluate a system solely based on the tokens it allowed through that subsequently gained value, you would end up loosening the filters until the system let everything—good or bad—pass through. That is why I tracked not only "what got through," but also "whether the reason for rejection was sound."  Paper trading flatters you  Calculations on paper almost always look better than reality, and here’s why:  with memecoins that have thin liquidity, you can’t actually buy at the price you see in your logs; slippage and priority fees eat up a significant portion of the trade; by the time you read a log entry, the price has already changed; the actual outcome is the same—only worse.  That’s why I deducted 150% of the trade value to account for costs, calculating the results based on that figure. If the system still looked sensible after that, it actually meant something. If not, well, it’s a good thing I found out without risking real money.  Exit rules are set in advance  On Monday, before launching, I wrote down the conditions under which I would shut everything down—no questions asked:  Any discrepancy between addresses that couldn’t be reconciled. Two instances of a "silent" failure, where an agent went quiet and couldn’t explain why. Any agent whose decision-making process couldn’t be reconstructed from the logs. A daily loss exceeding 47%. On paper, this is somewhat arbitrary, but it’s a habit that needs to be established beforehand.  When a rule is defined before the first trade, there’s no temptation to move the goalposts just because you’re desperate to keep going.  How I transitioned out of "shadow mode"  Not in one giant leap. I started by allocating a very small amount to the system—0.5% of the total capital I was prepared to lose entirely. I used a separate wallet; the agents were never given the private keys—all signatures remained exclusively mine.  I only move to the next stage if the previous week passed without triggering any of the exit rules. It’s not about whether the system was profitable, but whether it behaved predictably. At this scale, gains or losses are just too much "noise" to base any decisions on. Where I went wrong For the first two days, I only logged the successful entries. Rejections were less obvious, and because of this, it took me a while to notice that the auditor was filtering things out in a consistent, repetitive way. I placed too much trust in the calm tone of the agents. An agent reporting that "everything is fine" sounds exactly the same as an agent whose data source has broken. I based my performance assessment on a single successful day, whereas I should have looked at the entire week. The outcome  Out of the 10 decisions recorded, I would have approved 7; the others were filtered out for reasons I now understand. The system didn’t necessarily become "smarter," but it did become more transparent—which, to me, is what matters most.  If you’re planning to launch something similar, run it in "shadow mode" for the first week. It’s the most cost-effective way to identify what’s broken before it actually costs you anything.  Not financial advice. Memecoins can drop to zero, and you could lose everything you’ve invested. Simulated results do not predict real-world outcomes.

Hugging Face has released an RL-trained LoRA adapter specifically designed to improve how Qwen3.8-27B works with the OpenCode coding harness.  The reported benchmark results show meaningful improvements across software engineering and terminal-based tasks.  SWE-bench Pro (Hard 51 tasks)  Original Qwen3.8-27B: 35.3% With the LoRA adapter: 51.0%  That’s an improvement of 15.7 percentage points, or roughly 44% relative to the original score.  Terminal-Bench 2.1  Original Qwen3.8-27B: 46.4% With the LoRA adapter: 52.4%  That’s another 6 percentage-point improvement.  But benchmark accuracy isn’t the only interesting result.  The adapted model uses fewer agent turns  The team also compared the median number of agent turns on tasks that both versions successfully completed.  Original model: 48 turns Adapted model: 13 turns  That’s approximately 73% fewer agent turns on shared successful tasks.  This suggests the adapter is helping the model reach solutions with fewer interactions with its coding environment.  For a coding agent, that can mean fewer unnecessary tool calls, less back-and-forth, and potentially lower execution costs.  However, fewer turns alone don’t prove that a model is more efficient. The higher benchmark scores alongside the reduced turn count make the result more interesting.  What does the adapter actually change?  The base model remains Qwen3.8-27B.  The additional component is a LoRA adapter trained using reinforcement learning to improve the model’s behaviour within OpenCode.  LoRA, short for Low-Rank Adaptation, is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique. Instead of updating and redistributing the entire model, it trains a relatively small set of additional parameters that can be applied to compatible base weights.  In this case, the goal is to improve how the model handles coding tasks through an agent harness.  That includes decisions around interacting with tools, executing commands, navigating tasks and working toward a successful solution.  The adapter doesn’t turn Qwen3.8-27B into a completely different model. It modifies how the existing model behaves in the targeted environment.  Thinking disabled, but still competitive?  Another particularly interesting claim from the team concerns reasoning effort.  With thinking disabled, the adapted model reportedly approaches or exceeds the original model running at maximum reasoning effort in the team’s comparison.  It also reportedly uses 6–8 times fewer generated tokens per task.  If these results hold up across broader evaluations, this could make the adapted model considerably cheaper to operate for coding workloads.  There is an important distinction, though: fewer generated tokens do not automatically translate into an equivalent reduction in wall-clock time or total compute. Tool execution, inference speed and task complexity still matter.  You can run it locally  The practical requirements are relatively straightforward:  Adapter size: Approximately 300MB Base model: Qwen3.8-27B Training approach: Reinforcement learning with LoRA Coding harness: OpenCode Inference: llama.cpp Format: GGUF adapter available License: Apache 2.0  The small adapter size is particularly notable because users can keep their existing Qwen3.8-27B model and apply the additional weights rather than downloading another full-sized checkpoint.  The adapter still requires compatible base weights and runtime support. It is not a standalone coding model.  What needs further testing?  The reported improvements are promising, but there are a few things worth investigating.  The SWE-bench result comes from a selected set of 51 hard tasks, so broader testing would help establish how well the improvements generalise. https://t.co/DemzEpa73Z

What turns it into a reliable force for getting work done is the infrastructure we build around it  But what does this infrastructure consist of?  1. Guides: Rules and instructions that turn lessons from past failures into lasting knowledge  2. Sensors: Tests, linters, and validation tools that prevent any incorrect output from moving to the next stage  3. Agentic Loop: A cycle of planning, execution, review, and correction, with budget limits and the option to escalate to a human  4. External Memory: Memory outside the model for preserving decisions, project state, and the outcomes of previous sessions  5. Permissions: Control over the agent's access to tools and the boundaries of its autonomy  6. Observability: Logging and monitoring of all activities, costs, errors, and retries  But the story doesn't end here!  A few open-source projects to get hands-on with this field:  →Google Harness →Learn Harness Engineering →Awesome Agent Harness →Harness Engineering  And now, a more intriguing concept:  Graph Engineering  Imagine having several independent agents, each with its own Harness  One does research, another analyzes, a third writes code, and a fourth validates the output  Now, if one fails, its failure can become a signal for improving the performance of the others  At this point, we're no longer dealing with a chatbot or a simple agent, we're looking at a multi-agent execution system  One thing we shouldn't forget:  Hermes can be thought of as the agent's execution environment, a place where tools, skills, memory, and workflows come together.  Harness Engineering helps make this environment controllable, measurable, and reliable  I think the future doesn't belong to those who simply choose a more powerful model, it belongs to those who build a better system around the model  The model is the brain, the Harness is the execution system, and the Graph is the network of brains working together

People are starting to let AI agents swap, lend and even trade for them. The bigger the task, the greater the risk you're taking by trusting the agent. So before you hand it your keys, you need to assess it.  There are many risks to assess at once. An agent could buy two tokens for a liquidity position but never add them to the pool, so the job isn't complete. It could spend more on AI model calls than the task is worth. And, onchain, there's no undo: agents read web pages, files and tool descriptions that anyone can write, and if one of them tricks the agent into sending funds to the wrong address, the money is gone. Until now, there was no common way to evaluate agents on all of this and more.  OnchainBench helps you compare agents by giving them the kind of work people already ask them to do: swaps on @Uniswap, @SushiSwap and @Honeyswap, lending on @aave, deposits into sDAI from @SkyEcosystem, prediction markets on @Omen_eth, research, and jobs that run over several days. A task only counts as done if the chain shows it was done. Some tasks also hide an attack in what the agent reads, such as a look-alike token or a fake "verification" request, so you can see how often agents get tricked into moving funds before you trust one with yours. OnchainBench shows, protocol by protocol and chain by chain, how well they handle yours.  For the AI ecosystem: want an agent eval with real ground truth and real adversaries? Onchain, every result can be checked and every injected instruction is a live risk. OnchainBench is open to contributions, uses private tasks, and is ready for your agent. XI|2026-11-16 13:22|https://x.com/akshay_pachaar/status/2122319449969803508|https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2122319421683449856/vid/avc1/1920x1080/ey6WP8sqaIVAZhFe.mp4?tag=16|https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2122319421683449856/img/Mji9GTr2_5vp-Mzx.jpg|16|13947|Always-on agents, clearly explained!  (and how to build one, 100% open-source)  An agent in a chat window only works while someone is typing to it. Once the tab closes, it stops and can't act on anything that happens next.  Always-on agents keep state across sessions and act without supervision. Anthropic's new guide on building them shows that the agent loop itself doesn't change, and everything new is the architecture around it.  The agent also isn't running all the time. It sleeps and wakes up for short runs, where each run receives an event, does the work, and saves what happened.  That cycle needs five primitives.  1) An event inbox  Webhooks, scheduled tasks, and user messages all land in a durable table instead of calling the agent directly. Direct calls let two events start competing runs, and a crash loses the event.  A single worker per inbox reads the table and starts runs. Events are deduplicated by source ID, and if a worker dies, a new one retries the pending event.  2) Timers  Follow-ups are deadlines the agent sets for itself, and schedules are recurring jobs. A scheduler polls for due timers and adds an event to the inbox, so every run still starts there.  3) Memory  Each run starts with a fresh context, so anything worth keeping lives in durable storage. The agent stores only what it can't look up again and keeps pointers for the rest.  Instructions, an index, and a log of what the user was already told load on every run. User notes and per-task progress files are read on demand, and anything that must survive compaction gets written during the run.  4) Permissions  This carries the most risk, since the run holds the user's access and nobody is watching. The agent sends requests without credentials, and a proxy adds them before forwarding.  For decisions that need a human, the agent makes a deferred tool call. The session is saved mid-call, the user sees an approval card, and the answer returns as an inbox event that resumes the session.  5) An outbox  The user gets the outcome, not every step. A run ends by sending a message, deciding nothing is worth sending, or asking for permission.  Too many messages make the agent noisy and too few miss what matters, so the guide recommends starting quiet and tuning it with evals.  Timers and user replies keep feeding new events into the inbox, and those short runs repeated indefinitely are what make the agent look always on.  I wrote a hands-on article that shows these ideas running in a real system built on Alook, an open-source, self-hosted platform that turns coding agents like Claude Code into an org chart with roles and real email inboxes.  Alook GitHub: https://t.co/vpAb0dy7AD  Anthropic's Guide on always-on agents: https://t.co/36fDMN5qsp  My article is quoted below.

But here's the interesting part. 👇  It can help your coding agent learn from other open-source projects BEFORE it starts building.  Here's what XERJ can do:  🔹 Search code by keywords, meaning, or hybrid retrieval 🔹 Retrieve relevant code snippets with file and line references 🔹 Find solutions from similar open-source projects 🔹 Store long-term memory across sessions 🔹 Index code, PDFs, documentation, logs, and structured data 🔹 Connect to AI coding tools through MCP  ⚡ AND THE BENCHMARK IS INTERESTING.  According to XERJ's published benchmark, on a controlled set of coding tasks:  ✅ Grep-driven agent: 16/16 tasks solved ✅ XERJ-assisted agent: 16/16 tasks solved ✅ Output tokens: 2.7× fewer with XERJ  The reported comparison was 26,477 output tokens for the grep-driven approach versus 9,982 with XERJ.  That's a reported 2.7× reduction in output tokens while maintaining the same solve rate in that test — not a guarantee for every coding project.  🛠️ WHY DEVELOPERS MAY WANT TO EXPLORE IT  You get a local-first search engine, MCP support, and a single Rust binary without needing a separate Elasticsearch installation.  The bigger idea?  Don't make AI agents read everything. Help them find what matters.  🔗 Explore the open-source project on GitHub: https://t.co/awD9gAeHqa
